case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Precision Components (KPC) is a private limited company in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Freya Kestrel, it machines aerospace engine components for civil aircraft manufacturers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KPC plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC machining cell with automated inspection, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $24.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. KPC faces two problems: its defect rate has reached 4.2% with rising quality complaints, and labour turnover is increasing among CNC programmers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The new machining cell inspected 8,400 components last month at a defect rate of 4.2%, down from 6.5% a year ago, and each defective unit costs $28 to rework. Customer quality complaints have risen from 19 to 34 per month. Average order delivery lead time is 12 days. A survey of 250 aerospace buyers found that 68% rank on-time delivery as their top supplier criterion, and 57% would switch supplier after two late deliveries. A skills audit shows 18 of 60 production staff lack CNC programming certification; on-the-job training is available internally, while off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Precision Components as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.80 to $14.60 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across engineering. (3) Steel and aluminium input prices have risen 9.6% year-on-year, industrial producer inflation is 6.3%, and demand from aerospace manufacturers grew 4.1%.

questions.question_text: KPC plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC expansion with a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KPC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $270,000 of retained profit costs KPC no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the company already carries fixed costs of $300,000 a year and is servicing a $450,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on tackling the 4.2% defect rate, for example by cutting the $28-per-unit rework burden or funding the $1,100 CNC courses, helping KPC hold its $24.00 selling price for aerospace buyers who rank on-time delivery first.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the $720,000 machining cell is not endangered if the 68% of surveyed buyers who demand on-time delivery are disappointed and orders slip. It also preserves the ownership and control of founder Freya Kestrel: no lender can impose conditions on how the flat, democratically led team runs the new CNC cell, letting KPC react quickly to the 57% of buyers who say they would switch supplier after two late deliveries. Retained profit therefore speeds the decision and keeps control local.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KPC's costs, defect rate, finance and ownership.

questions.question_text: KPC is promoting its new precision-machined aerospace components. Consider a national trade-press advertising campaign, sponsorship of an aerospace industry exhibition, or targeted email marketing to known OEM buyers. Which should KPC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-press campaign: Advertisements in aerospace magazines would build wide awareness of KPC's new CNC-machined components across the whole industry, reinforcing the 8,400 components inspected monthly and the fall from 6.5% to 4.2% in defects. However, print is costly, has a long lead time and reaches many firms outside KPC's civil-aircraft niche; with a $720,000 expansion and fixed costs of $300,000 a year, much of the spend would be wasted on readers who never buy engine components.

Exhibition sponsorship: Sponsoring an aerospace trade exhibition gives face-to-face credibility and direct access to procurement teams, valuable because 68% of 250 surveyed buyers rank on-time delivery first and 57% would switch after two late deliveries, so trust must be built personally. The drawbacks are high stand fees, staff time away from the 40,000-unit production target and results that depend on a single event; for a 60-employee firm with a $450,000 loan this is a large, lumpy risk.

Targeted email marketing: Sending focused technical messages to KPC's known OEM buyer list is cheap, immediate and measurable, and can carry the 12-day delivery lead time and quality data straight to the engineers who decide. It lacks the brand reach of print and the personal trust of an exhibition, and works only where contact data is accurate, but its cost per qualified enquiry is far lower than either alternative.

Recommendation: KPC should choose targeted email marketing, supported later by a small exhibition presence. It reaches exactly the civil-aircraft buyers who matter, can be justified against $300,000 fixed costs and a $450,000 loan, and directly communicates the reliability message the survey identifies. National trade-press advertising is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and full exhibition sponsorship is rejected as too costly and disruptive for a 60-staff firm; email can be scaled up once the machining cell proves its 4.2% defect improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to KPC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of KPC and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to KPC with a justified recommendation explaining why trade-press advertising and exhibition sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: KPC's labour turnover is rising among CNC programmers and its defect rate has reached 4.2%. Explain two benefits for KPC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives KPC's 60 employees a real voice in how the new CNC machining cell is organised, which helps satisfy higher social and esteem needs and lifts job satisfaction. Programmers who help set inspection routines and shift patterns are more likely to stay, directly reducing the labour turnover that is losing scarce CNC skills and forcing repeated $1,100 off-the-job training spending.

Point 2: Consulting the people who operate the machines generates practical ideas for reducing the 4.2% defect rate and the $28-per-unit rework cost, because operators see faults before managers do. Higher involvement also strengthens commitment to the 12-day delivery promise, which matters because 68% of 250 surveyed buyers rank on-time delivery first and 57% would switch after two late deliveries. In a flat structure, democratic decision-making fits KPC's culture and supports founder Freya Kestrel's goal of protecting the $720,000 investment without adding supervisory layers. That stability matters when 18 staff still need CNC certification and the new cell depends on their skills.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to KPC's turnover, defect rate, delivery promise and costs.

questions.question_text: KPC must upskill 18 production staff to operate the new CNC machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should KPC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the machining cell is directly relevant to KPC's own CNC machines and inspection standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 8,400 components inspected each month and the improvement from 6.5% to 4.2% defects. It also suits the 12-day delivery lead time because nobody leaves the line. The weaknesses are that trainers are themselves production staff whose output suffers, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate, a concern when 68% of surveyed aerospace buyers demand reliable delivery and may audit supplier competence.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $1,100 per employee gives structured, up-to-date CNC programming skills and a recognised certificate for all 18 staff, costing $19,800 in total, small beside the $720,000 expansion. It removes staff from production, however, reducing short-term capacity and risking the 40,000-unit target, and the generic syllabus may not match KPC's exact machines, so follow-up on site would still be required. With labour turnover already rising, sending newly trained staff off site also risks losing them.

Decision: KPC should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college top-ups for the most senior programmers. On-the-job training is machine-specific, avoids the $19,800 fee and protects output while the defect rate is being brought under control. Full off-the-job training is rejected because losing 18 staff from the line would threaten the 12-day delivery promise and the $450,000 loan service, and KPC can add formal certification later once the cell is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KPC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of KPC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods applied to KPC with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KPC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 10,000 units vs 40,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $300,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $720,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $21.50 to tackle the 4.2% defect rate.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($24.00 − $14.00) = $300,000 ÷ $10.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $24.00 − $14.00 = $10.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KPC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. KPC's managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 40,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 10,000 units, to judge whether the new $720,000 CNC cell is used enough to justify the $450,000 loan.
2. Contribution per unit of $10.00 lets managers model a discount negotiated with aerospace buyers, for example a 5% price cut to $22.80 would reduce contribution to $8.80, and still check that the $300,000 fixed costs are covered.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $300,000 and contribution of $10.00 helps set the volume needed to service the loan and decide whether to bid for extra demand hinted at by 4.1% growth in aerospace orders.
4. Managers can use average total cost ($300,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $14.00 = $21.50 a unit) to benchmark the 4.2% defect rate and $28 rework cost quarter by quarter and press suppliers on the 9.6% rise in steel and aluminium input prices.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii), max 4.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KPC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KPC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.62 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.06 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.15 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $210,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $405,000; 2025 current assets = $165,000 + $195,000 + $70,000 = $430,000. Short-term cover for 2024 is $405,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.62 and for 2025 is $430,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.87. Excluding inventories, ($405,000 − $140,000) ÷ $250,000 = 1.06 in 2024 and ($430,000 − $165,000) ÷ $230,000 = 1.15 in 2025.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has strengthened on both measures. Current liabilities fell from $250,000 to $230,000 while current assets rose from $405,000 to $430,000, so the 2025 cover is more comfortable. The acid test also improved, meaning KPC is less dependent on selling inventory to pay debts, important while it services a $450,000 bank loan and funds a $720,000 CNC cell. However, inventories rose from $140,000 to $165,000, tying up cash, and receivables, though lower at $195,000, remain large for a 60-staff firm; if buyers delay payment the stronger position could quickly weaken. The new $720,000 CNC cell has also raised non-current assets from $1,600,000 to $2,150,000, so part of the improved liquidity is being used to fund long-term capacity rather than left as spare cash.

Conclusion: KPC's financial position has improved. Both cover measures are higher and the improvement does not rely on stock. The residual risk is higher inventories and slow receivables, so management should tighten credit control before further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether KPC's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KPC of introducing automated optical inspection to reduce its 4.2% defect rate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automated optical inspection would detect faults far more consistently than manual checks, directly attacking the 4.2% defect rate and the $28-per-unit rework cost seen across the 8,400 components inspected each month. Better quality supports the 68% of 250 surveyed aerospace buyers who rank on-time delivery first, because fewer defects mean less rework delaying the 12-day lead time, and it protects the $720,000 investment in the new CNC cell by ensuring output meets civil-aircraft standards.

Disadvantage: Automated inspection needs further capital and technical skill to install and maintain, on top of the $450,000 bank loan and fixed costs of $300,000 a year, and KPC already has a skills gap with 18 of 60 staff lacking CNC certification. If the system generates false rejects, output could fall below the 40,000-unit target and the 57% of buyers who would switch after two late deliveries might do so. Software and sensor upkeep would also raise fixed costs before the 4.2% improvement is proven.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KPC's quality data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in steel and aluminium input costs will affect KPC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If KPC's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest against $300,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is zero. Higher base rates may still make aerospace buyers delay orders and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but KPC can cap this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.60 per hour): With a workforce of 60, many machining and packing roles are hourly paid, so this rise feeds into wage bills. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest comparison is with given productivity, 40,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 667 units per worker. A wage rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost pushes up the $21.50 average total cost and squeezes the $10.00 contribution per unit.

Input cost inflation (9.6% steel and aluminium): KPC's $14.00 variable cost per unit includes metal, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.6% that would add 9.6% × $14.00 = $1.34 per unit; at 40,000 units that is about $54,000 a year (40,000 × $1.34). Even a smaller $1.00-per-unit rise would cost $40,000 a year, cutting contribution from $10.00 towards $9.00 and threatening the $720,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact: it compounds on every one of the 40,000 units, directly eroding the $10.00 contribution that services the $450,000 loan, and it cannot be removed by fixing a rate or by productivity alone. The interest rise is small and fixable; the wage rise matters but depends on hours and productivity KPC can manage. Input inflation therefore bites deepest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KPC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KPC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to KPC with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
